name: Buôn Đôn
summary: A village on the Serepok River, once famous for catching and training wild elephants. Today it is a place to learn about M'nông and Lao culture and the elephants of the Yok Đôn forest.

hero.alt: The Serepok River at Buôn Đôn

eras.label: c. 1900
eras.title: The elephant hunters
eras.text: Buôn Đôn grew as a trading village where M'nông, Lao and Ê Đê people met. Its hunters were famous for catching wild elephants and training them to carry loads and work in the forest.

image.file: DKoehl Buon Don elephant hunter cemetry 2011.jpg
image.alt: The cemetery of the elephant hunters

eras.label: 1990s
eras.title: A national park
eras.text: The dry forest of Yok Đôn, next to the village, became a national park to protect its wild elephants, deer and birds. Catching wild elephants is now forbidden.

image.alt: Forest in Yok Đôn National Park

eras.label: 2020s
eras.title: Watching, not riding
eras.text: Elephant rides were long a tourist attraction here. In recent years local projects have moved towards letting visitors watch elephants walk, bathe and feed freely.

eras.label: Today
eras.title: Bridges over the Serepok
eras.text: Bamboo suspension bridges cross the river between islands of old trees, and visitors stay in stilt houses to try highland food and hear the gongs.

story.title: The king of the elephant hunters

image.file: DKoehl Buon Don elephant hunter cemetry 2011.jpg

story.narration: The most famous man in Buôn Đôn's history was Y Thu Knul, known as Khunjunob. Born in the 19th century, he is said to have caught hundreds of wild elephants in his long life. Stories say he caught a rare white elephant and gave it to the King of Siam, who honoured him with the title Khunjunob, 'king of elephant hunters'. His tomb stands in the village cemetery, where the graves of hunters are decorated with carved wooden figures.

story.title: Blessing the elephants

image.file: DKoehl Buon Don Mnong elephant blessing ceremony 2012.jpg

story.narration: For the M'nông, an elephant is part of the family. When a new elephant was captured, or before a long journey, the owners held a ceremony to ask the spirits to keep it healthy. A shaman offered rice wine, a chicken or a pig, and spoke to the elephant and the spirits together. The ceremony is still held today, and visitors are sometimes invited to watch. It shows the bond between people and the great animals of the forest.

story.title: Coffee of the highlands
story.narration: The French brought coffee to the Central Highlands in the early 20th century, and the red basalt soil around Buôn Ma Thuột proved perfect for it. Most of what grows here is robusta: strong and bitter. Vietnamese drink it dripped slowly through a small metal filter, the phin, often with sweetened condensed milk, hot or over ice. In February and March the coffee trees flower white, and the air smells of jasmine.

guide.price: Ticket for the tourist area and bamboo bridges; small extra fees for some activities.

do: Wear shoes with grip on the bamboo bridges.
Visit Khunjunob's tomb in the village.
Try highland food in a stilt house.
dont: Ride elephants or feed them sugar.
Swim in the Serepok; currents are strong.

tips.title: Highland food
tips.text: Grilled chicken, bamboo-tube rice and rice wine; and of course Buôn Ma Thuột coffee.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: About 45 km from Buôn Ma Thuột, which has an airport.

tips.title: Nearby
tips.text: Dray Nur and Dray Sáp waterfalls on the Serepok, and the coffee museum in Buôn Ma Thuột.
